title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
hook: a grieving groom vows to kill every snake he meets, until a harmless one speaks up and teaches him not to harm
carry: we share the name, nothing else
tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Adi Parva: Uttanka, the stolen earrings, and a grudge carried all the way to King Janamejaya. Did someone hand you their anger? Day six hundred ninety-nine.

The wedding has been set. The bride, Pramadvara, is out with her friends, and she steps on a snake she doesn't see. It bites her, and she dies. The groom is Ruru, a young man of the family of the sage Bhrigu. He goes off alone into the forest and weeps. Then a messenger of the gods comes to him with an offer: she can live again, if he gives her half of his own life. He gives it. She wakes. They marry. It could end there, happily. It doesn't.
screen: `A BRIDE, A HIDDEN SNAKE.` → `HALF HIS LIFE FOR HERS.` → `IT DOESN'T END THERE.`

segments.voice: Ruru makes a vow. From now on, whenever he sees a snake, he will kill it. And he keeps the vow. He carries a heavy stick, and he strikes the snakes he finds. One day he comes on an old snake lying on the ground, of a kind called a dundubha, and he raises the stick. The snake speaks. I've done you no harm, it says. Why strike me? Ruru answers that a snake killed his wife, so he kills snakes. The dundubha answers: we're not the ones who bite. We share the name snake with them, and nothing else. Then it tells Ruru who it really is: a sage, cursed to live in this shape until the day it met him. Standing as a man again, the sage gives Ruru a teaching. Not harming living beings, he says, is the highest dharma. A man of a priestly family should be known for gentleness and forgiveness, not for the stick. Notice where the Adi Parva puts this. We're inside the frame of a king trying to burn the snakes. And before we get to that fire, the poem lets a creature in a snake's shape speak for ahimsa, not harming. Ruru's grief was real. His rage was real. But he had turned one bite into a war on a whole kind of creature. The sage even points ahead: he mentions Janamejaya's snake sacrifice, and that it was stopped. Then he's gone. Ruru goes home and asks his father to tell him the rest. And that's how the poem gets us back to the fire: a grieving man, freshly taught mercy, asking how a king's war on the snakes began and ended.
screen: `RURU'S VOW: KILL EVERY SNAKE.` · `WE'RE NOT THE ONES WHO BITE.` · `A SAGE UNDER A CURSE.` · `NOT HARMING: THE HIGHEST DHARMA.` · then, large: `AHIMSA.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come and go on its own for a moment. Bring to mind one hurt that came from one person, or one thing. Now notice whether it has spread: from one dog to all dogs, one driver to all drivers, one person to everyone who looks like them. Don't argue with it. Just see the line between the one that bit and the ones that never did. Let the breath come in on the one, and go out on the many. The bell holds the time.
Adi Parva. The opening book, where a harmless snake teaches a grieving man not to harm.
Your line: we share the name, nothing else. Today, catch one moment when one bad experience starts speaking for a whole group. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Ahimsa, not harming living beings, is taught in Hindu texts beyond this one, and some Hindus practice it through vegetarian diet, care for animals, and restraint in speech.

myth: Ruru vowed to kill every snake he met
after his bride was bitten, he struck the snakes he found with a heavy stick.
the dundubha was really a sage under a curse
meeting Ruru freed him, and he stood as a man again.
the sage told Ruru to keep his vow
he taught him that not harming living beings is the highest dharma.

fork.setup: you're the old dundubha. a man with a stick is about to kill you for something another snake did. what do you do?
options: speak up: you're not the one who bit his wife.
lie still and hope he passes.
fork.reveal: the dundubha speaks: we share the name snake and nothing else. then, freed from its curse, it teaches him ahimsa.

original.note: Sanskrit ahiṃsā, not harming: the teaching the freed sage gives Ruru.

trapdoor: what you thought: a side story before the real one.
what it means: before the snake fire, the poem lets a snake speak for not harming.
what a scholar hears: the Puloma section: Ruru, Pramadvara and the dundubha, whose teaching on ahimsa turns the story toward Astika.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Puloma Parva (Ruru and Pramadvara; Ruru and the dundubha)

notes: All paraphrase. The dundubha's teaching is rendered as 'not harming living beings is the highest dharma' (ahimsa paramo dharmah in the Sanskrit); confirm the wording against Ganguli.
Half of Ruru's life given for Pramadvara is in the text; confirm.
The freed sage (Sahasrapat in the text) is left unnamed; his mention of Janamejaya's sacrifice and its ending, and Ruru then asking his father, should be checked.
howItsDone mentions vegetarian diet and care for animals as ways some Hindus practice ahimsa; confirm phrasing.

Editor (y3 audit): cut 'asleep' (not certain in the text); the ahimsa teaching is now credited to 'a creature in a snake's shape' since the sage speaks it after his release; varied the practice opener and cut a repeated 'if you pray' line; cut the sweeping 'found across Hindu texts' and the unsourced retelling claim in howItsDone.
